entries.title: Trump’s Anti-Fraud Crusade Casts a Long Shadow Over Minnesota Governor’s Race
entries.summary: Whoever controls the governor’s mansion next year will contend with fallout from the White House’s large withdrawal of federal Medicaid funding earlier this year.
entries.content:
Republicans have made Minnesota central to their crusade against fraud in federal government programs. Now, both gubernatorial candidates are arguing they’re better equipped to right the ship.

The stakes are high for Minnesota’s federal programs: The White House is currently withholding close to $200 million in federal Medicaid payments over fraud concerns in Minnesota’s public health programs, and Trump has accused outgoing Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, of allowing the state to become a “hub of fraudulent money laundering activity.” The state’s large Somali population also faced an intense immigration crackdown operation last winter, with officials in part citing allegations of fraud in public programs.

Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar on Tuesday tried to make an early entry in the lane Republicans have dominated for the last year as voters turn to the general election. Her first general election TV ad promises “a top-to-bottom audit of state government” to rid the state of “the waste and the fraud and the abuse” — a phrase that’s typically been used by conservatives, including the Trump officials who have rescinded the state’s federal funding.

“She knows it's a massive issue,” Amy Frederiksen, a Republican strategist and former state Senate majority leader, told NOTUS. Frederiksen says Democrats across the country haven’t been as vocal about combatting fraud, but “sometimes there's just local issues that rise up that even obscure some of the national pressures.”

Republican nominee Lisa Demuth — who has made fighting fraud a legislative priority during her time as state House speaker — says she’ll implement an updated anti-fraud plan during her first 90 days as governor. She also proposes firing all existing commissioners and replacing them with experts who are “committed to ending the culture of fraud,” restructuring state program eligibility requirements and establishing an independent state inspector general’s office.

Throughout her campaign, Demuth has tied Klobuchar to Walz, saying the senator’s tenure would be like a “Walz third term.” The governor dropped his bid for another term amid ongoing criticism for his administration’s handling of fraud in Minnesota’s state programs, and did not endorse Klobuchar in the primaries.

“By finally cleaning up the fraud and working with the federal government, I will be able to lift the federal freeze that’s been impacting the legitimate providers harmed by the failed leadership of Tim Walz and Amy Klobuchar,” Demuth said during a Tuesday news conference.

Demuth is likely to keep trying to tie her opponent to Walz, Frederiksen said — but the link might not resonate with voters because she “wasn't overseeing programs and these departments” while serving the state in D.C.

As a senator, Klobuchar says she successfully pushed for more prosecutors to handle cases related to the Feeding Our Future scandal, in which a child-nutrition program submitted fraudulent records to secure more than $240 million in federal funds.

“While others were just talking about fraud — I took action,” she wrote in a Tuesday post on X.

Last December, conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley posted a viral video alleging sweeping fraud at daycare centers run by the Somali community in Minnesota, and the state saw a surge in federal law enforcement presence soon after. Demuth said Minnesota’s Republican caucus had worked directly with Shirley and agency whistleblowers “to get the information out to the public and to hold the Walz administration accountable.”

Fraud has since become an increasingly salient issue for state voters, with 81% of respondents saying they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about the level of fraud in state social services programs in a June poll. The same poll showed 45% of likely voters trusted Republicans to combat fraud, while 38% picked Democrats.

While Klobuchar had maintained a close friendship with Walz for years — including introducing the then-vice presidential candidate at the 2024 DNC — she began to distance herself as the governor’s political profile soured. Throughout her gubernatorial campaign, Klobuchar has contrasted their records to defy Republicans’ attempts to tie her to Walz’s fraud troubles.

“You are right to be angry about the fraud. It is unacceptable and it must end. It should never have happened to begin with,” Klobuchar said at a May news conference announcing her anti-fraud plan.

As governor, Klobuchar says she’ll establish a state “Do Not Pay” database to automatically block entities convicted of fraud from accessing grants or contracts, conduct unannounced inspections of groups receiving funds and modernize state technology systems. She also supports creating an inspector general’s office to coordinate across agencies.

Frederiksen thinks speaking out against fraud is “a message that works dually” for both parties. Fighting fraud involves both Republicans’ desire to protect taxpayer money and Democrats’ priority of safeguarding federal assistance programs, she said.

“I just don't understand why the Democrats haven't been more vocal on it, and I think that Senator Klobuchar must feel the same because I think the message works on a lot of levels,” Frederiksen said. “It's certainly not just a GOP message, or shouldn't be, but it has been.”

entries.title: Local Media Mogul Beats Trump’s Pick in Crowded Florida House Race
entries.summary: The Florida race included two former members of Congress hoping to rehabilitate their political careers.
entries.content:
Jim Schwartzel was projected to win the Republican primary for Florida’s 19th Congressional District, prevailing in a crowded race for Rep. Byron Donalds’ open seat, which he opted to vacate in order to mount a run for governor.

The Associated Press called the race Tuesday for Schwartzel, a conservative local media mogul, who bested nearly a dozen candidates — including President Donald Trump’s pick, Catalina Lauf, and two former members of Congress with controversial tenures.

As the Republican nominee, Schwartzel will face Democrat Victor Arias in November. Schwartzel is likely to become the next representative for the district rated “Solid R” by the Cook Political Report.

Schwartzel spent nearly $1.9 million through July 29, according to Federal Elections Commission totals. He had raised concerns about his opponents’ lack of local ties to southwest Florida, leaning heavily on his status as one of the few candidates who is a lifelong resident of the state.

Lauf, a former Commerce Department adviser during Trump’s first term, earned the second-highest vote share after spending just $1.6 million on her campaign. She received a last-minute endorsement from Trump on Aug. 13, and earned the support of Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna.

Lauf faced criticism for recently moving to Florida from her home state of Illinois, where she ran for Congress in 2022. Her lack of ties to the district became a scandal of sorts in the waning days of the primary campaign after an audio clip showed Lauf struggling to answer questions about local officials in her newly adopted city of Bonita Springs.

Many of the frontrunners’ foes previously held elected positions in other states, before recently moving to Florida.

Former Illinois state Sen. Jim Oberweis had the largest war chest in the race with $5.3 million, nearly all of which came from a personal loan to the campaign.

Former New York Rep. Chris Collins, whom Trump pardoned in 2020 after he served two months of his 26-month sentence for insider trading and lying to the FBI, was also in the running. He spent more than $2.4 million of his entirely self-funded campaign of $3.4 million.

Former Rep. Madison Cawthorn, who served one term in Congress for North Carolina before losing his reelection bid in 2023, also moved to the district to run for the seat. The House Ethics Committee had admonished Cawthorn over accusations that he improperly promoted cryptocurrency just before he lost reelection to Congress. He had also faced sexual misconduct allegations from his past and legal troubles for bringing a loaded gun to an airport, as well as ticketed for excessive speeding and charged with driving on a revoked license.

Cawthorn loaned $800,000 to his campaign, which spent more than $720,000 on the race.

Other candidates included former congressional staffer Ola Hawatmeh, pardoned Jan. 6 rioter John Strand, businessman Greg “Tex” Burkowski, Marine Corps veteran Mike Pedersen and nurse Linda Sawyer.

This story has been updated with the race call for the Democratic nominee.

entries.title: Cory Mills Loses Primary as He Faces Investigations Into His Behavior
entries.summary: The Florida Republican’s defeat ends a career in Congress defined by controversy.
entries.content:
Embattled Rep. Cory Mills of Florida was projected to lose his reelection bid to a former local television news host amid a growing list of scandals and investigations that affected his standing within the House Republican Conference.

The Associated Press called the race Tuesday for Ryan Elijah, who had the backing of some members of the Florida congressional delegation and handily outraised the Mills in recent months.

The two-term congressman’s defeat ends a career in Congress that was defined by controversy. Mills is currently under criminal investigation by the Justice Department, which is looking into his personal and campaign finances, a source familiar told NOTUS.

He is also under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for a range of allegations, including domestic violence against his partner in his Washington, D.C., apartment, campaign-finance violations and accusations that his company held government contracts while he was a sitting member of Congress.

Mills has remained defiant and denied the allegations and has said he has no knowledge of a DOJ investigation into him.

On top of these investigations, Mills has run into other issues throughout his years in Congress.

NOTUS first reported in 2025 about uncertainties surrounding Mills’ military service record. Five people who served with Mills in Iraq — including two men Mills is credited with saving on official military documents — said they have no recollection of Mills being involved in the incidents.

NOTUS also reported last year that Mills was caught with sex workers while on a rescue mission in Tbilisi, Georgia, in 2021 when he was a congressional candidate. He appeared to travel on to Afghanistan separate from the rest of the group, who were enraged by Mills’ behavior given the sensitive nature of the mission, sources told NOTUS.

The controversy surrounding Mills got so intense that even some of his own Republican colleagues sought to expel him from Congress. Some members of the Florida delegation, led by Rep. Mike Haridopolos, endorsed Elijah over him.

Mills also struggled to raise money — he brought in only $59,000 in the second quarter of the year, according to Federal Election Commission numbers, and only had $81,000 on hand.
entries.author: Reese Gorman

entries.title: The Anti-Abortion Movement Is Split Over Sen. Darline Graham
entries.summary: One anti-abortion leader told NOTUS she has “real concerns” that Graham will not be “a pro-life fighter.”
entries.content:
Sen. Darline Graham’s lack of legislative record is threatening her chances in the South Carolina Senate Republican runoff, specifically on an issue that her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, dominated: ending abortion.

“One of the lessons that’s been very clear to pro-life activists and really conservative party activists over the last few months in the U.S. Senate is we need people who have got our backs and are true believers and are going to get things done and advance our agenda,” Kristan Hawkins, president of the prominent anti-abortion group Students for Life Action, told NOTUS.

But, Hawkins added, she has “real concerns about if [Graham is] really going to be a pro-life fighter in Washington, D.C.”

SFLA endorsed Rep. Ralph Norman in the runoff, citing his track record introducing and supporting anti-abortion legislation in the House and his involvement in supporting a lawsuit to defund Planned Parenthood. Hawkins’ group, which was the first national anti-abortion group to weigh in on the race, said Norman signed its candidate pledge committing to back anti-abortion priorities.

The organization reached out to Graham multiple times while it was deciding which candidate to endorse but received no response.

“We have not heard back from her team. Apparently, she thinks she’s got bigger fish to fry,” Hawkins said.

The endorsement was a blow for Graham, whose standing as a relatively unknown senator has led to a divide within the Republican Party over who to support in the runoff, even with President Donald Trump backing her. She was appointed to the Senate last month after the sudden death of her brother, who was viewed as a reliable anti-abortion vote over his three decades in Congress.

“Lindsey Graham fought for life, and he fought to see the end of abortion,” Hawkins said. “I don’t think the torch has been passed.”

Darline Graham received 33% of the vote in the special Republican primary earlier this month, the most votes among Republicans in the race. However, since she failed to get a majority of the votes, Graham and Norman, who received 25%, will face off in a runoff election next Tuesday.

Now, a rift in the anti-abortion movement is playing out over who its best advocate is.

Just a day after SFLA announced its endorsement, a decision that Hawkins said she knew would be seen as “controversial,” another major anti-abortion group, Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, backed Graham.

“I used to know Sen. Darline Graham through her brother, the great Senate pro-life champion and my good friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham. But now, I’ve gotten to know her directly for who she is. Her pro-life values are passionate and deeply rooted in principle,” Marjorie Dannenfelser, SBA’s president, said in a statement. “I urge all South Carolinians to vote for her.”

In a press release touting the support, Graham said she was “proud to be the most pro-life candidate in this race.” She bragged about the support in Tuesday’s debate against Norman, saying she was “honored and excited” to be backed by the group.

SBA’s endorsement was not surprising. The organization had a close relationship with Lindsey Graham and had already committed to deploying its grassroots to South Carolina as part of its $80 million planned spending this election cycle.

Hawkins said that last week she spoke to staff from the National Right to Life Committee, another big anti-abortion group that often gets involved in political races, and told them about Graham’s donation to Shealy. The NRLC told NOTUS that it planned to endorse in the race, but it did not reveal which candidate it would be backing nor say when it would be announced.

But previous donations tie Graham to abortion rights supporters.

She accepted a $10,000 donation from Denali Leadership PAC, a leadership PAC affiliated with Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), one of only two Republican senators who support abortion rights. In 2020, Graham donated $100 to former Republican South Carolina state Sen. Katrina Shealy, who gained national attention in 2022 when she played a key role in blocking a near-total abortion ban from becoming law in the state.

The Daily Beast, which was the first to report the Shealy donation, said that shortly after the outlet reached out to Graham’s campaign for comment on the story, her office posted on X that the senator was “proud to be pro-life and to stand up for the unborn” and endorsed seven anti-abortion bills in the Senate.

None of the bills she endorsed are abortion bans.

When asked about the post, Hawkins told NOTUS that Graham “didn’t support the Life at Conception Act,” a bill that would grant embryos personhood rights, effectively outlawing abortion. Hawkins added that SFLA had reached out to Graham about potentially having her be the lead Senate sponsor for the “Clean Water for All Life Act,” a bill which would restrict access to abortion pills and has been introduced in the House.

Graham’s campaign declined to respond to NOTUS’ detailed questions, including what her stances on abortion are and whether she agreed with Shealy. The former state senator told The New York Times that she and Graham are close friends but never spoke about politics, but Graham told reporters on Monday that they were not friends and said she was “definitely pro-life.”

The criticism over her record has seemingly gotten to Graham’s campaign.

On Tuesday afternoon, Graham spokesperson Abby Zilch posted on X that Norman had donated $1,000 to former Democratic South Carolina state Rep. Leon Stavrinakis. In 2022, he voted against a six-week abortion ban in the state.

But Zilch did not mention that the donation was from 2015, when Stavrinakis was running for Charleston mayor in a nonpartisan election against another Democrat, John Tecklenburg. Tecklenburg, who was backed by progressives, ultimately won that race.

Norman and his campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ requests for comment over text and email.
entries.author: Oriana González

entries.title: What to Do In the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 21)
entries.summary: The National Book Festival, Improvapolozza and the return of live music at the Carter Barron Amphitheater.
entries.content:
Thursday 


Washington Improv Theater’s Improvapolooza 2026 
Studio Theatre, 1501 14th St. NW, 7:30 p.m., $25 for a nightly pass 

Thursday marks Day 2 of this five-day festival, which features hundreds of local improv pros and amateurs (many of them federal employees) aiming to entertain, as long as you supply a country, a favorite food and the name of your ex-boyfriend. Thursday’s lineup includes a cast of former athletes, several vampire-themed sessions and a sketch entirely sung a cappella.

JazzDC AllStars at Carter Barron Amphitheater
4850 Colorado Ave. NW, 6 p.m., $15

For 10 years, Rock Creek Park’s Carter Barron Amphitheater has lain fallow like a cursed castle in a modern fairytale, surrounded by chain-link fence and overgrown with plants. That all changes this weekend, when live music returns to the venue for the first time since 2016. The Rock Creek Conservancy, D.C. Jazz Festival and Washington Performing Arts teamed up to revive the amphitheater with a trio of shows. Sunday’s show is already sold out, but tickets remain for the JazzDC Allstars on Thursday and Sylver Logan Sharp and the Groovement ALLstars on Friday.

More to explore: “Wine and Design” origami night at the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum

Friday 


Ledisi: For Dinah at Strathmore
5301 Tuckerman Lane, North Bethesda, 8 p.m., $29 to $139 

The versatile vocalist Ledisi has portrayed gospel legend Mahalia Jackson twice in films and received a Grammy nomination for covering songs made famous by Nina Simone. Now she’s honoring jazz chanteuse Dinah Washington, and touring in support of her 2025 album, “For Dinah.” Produced by “Jazz Night in America” host Christian McBride, this album of sultry night music includes standards like “Caravan,” “What a Difference a Day Makes” and “This Bitter Earth.” She will be performing at Strathmore on Friday and Saturday.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“Michael” screening at Films at the Stone
1964 Independence Ave. SW, 8 p.m., free

Outdoor movie season continues this weekend as “Michael” screens at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial on Friday night. The Michael Jackson biopic released this year focuses mostly on the singer’s musical milestones, and there’s no more thrilling way to see the film than projected onto the memorial’s flat side, along the Tidal Basin.

More to explore: “Beltway Bungalow” vintage fair in Alexandria

Saturday 


National Book Festival 
Washington Convention Center, 801 Allen Y. Lew Place NW, 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., free (tickets required)

This annual celebration of literature is as much about books as it is celebrities with books to promote. This year’s A-list authors include “Wicked” star Cynthia Erivo debuting a memoir; SNL alum Kate McKinnon chatting about her foray into young adult fiction and filmmaker Martin Scorsese talking about — well, there doesn’t seem to be a book involved but there’s always “Taxi Driver.” Don’t take kids to that, but younger readers will enjoy read-aloud events on the Story District stage. For Orioles fans, owner David Rubenstein will sit down with announcer Kevin Brown. But be forewarned: Rubenstein will not be signing copies of his book “Inside the Owner’s Box,” probably because he doesn’t want to hear your thoughts on the Adley Rutschman trade.

Richard O’Brien’s “The Rocky Horror Show” 
Monumental Theatre Company at Dance Place, 3225 8th St. NE, 8 p.m. $45

You’ve seen the movie — maybe you’re even sung along at one of those late-night screenings — but have you ever seen “Rocky Horror Show” live? Now’s your chance, especially if the current Broadway run is beyond your budget. Monumental Theatre Company’s marquee event is its annual summer musical, and this year it’s offering a cult classic staged as an immersive cabaret. The Brookland venue Dance Place remains transformed into Dr. Frank-N-Furter's laboratory through Sept. 6.

More to explore: “Summer Saturdays” at George Mason’s Gunston Hall

Sunday 


“The Notebook” at The National Theatre
1321 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m., $81 to $223

May we suggest taking Mom to brunch, then to The National Theatre for a Sunday matinee performance of “The Notebook”? The mid-aughts indie pop ingénue Ingrid Michaelson adapted the 2004 film, which was already an adaptation of the Nicholas Sparks novel, into a Broadway musical that drew mixed reviews. “What makes you sigh and weep may leave the person next to you bored and stony,” opined New York Times critic Jesse Green. The tour runs at The National through Aug. 30. Grab the tissues (just in case) and see if watching lovers embrace as the rain falls onstage turns on the waterworks for you (or your mom).

“A Very Laufey Day”
Candlelight concerts at National City Christian Church, 5 Thomas Circle NW, 6:45 and 8:45 p.m., $52 to $105

The Icelandic singer Laufey is not performing Sunday at National City Christian Church (which also functions as a rental venue), but the former DMV resident did personally curate this tribute performance. Surrounded by onstage candles, the Listeo String Quartet will perform 21st century torch songs including “Dreamer,” “Lover Girl” and “Let You Break My Heart Again.”

More to explore: Perreito and Coffee social at Llamabar
entries.author: Rebecca Ritzel

entries.title: Working Hard or Hardly Working?
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 19, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Six current and former D.C. police employees stand accused of pocketing nearly half a million dollars combined for overtime they did not actually work, NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright reports.

A judge signed arrest warrants for all six, D.C.’s top prosecutors announced Tuesday. They will be charged with fraud, theft, forgery and uttering (a term we just learned; it means presenting a document one knows is fake or forged).

Prosecutors allege that the employees routinely submitted false information about hours they worked in 2024. In some cases, they claimed to have been working overtime while they were actually traveling outside of the District, according to prosecutors. The highest-earning of the group, a former sergeant, received nearly $175,000 from the alleged scheme.

The arrests come as D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department is struggling to curb soaring overtime costs and grappling with a 50-year staffing low. For many officers, overtime has become an increasingly common and exhausting necessity.

The fraud alleged here represents a small fraction of overtime spending at the department, which reached a whopping $134 million last fiscal year.





DEEP DIVE

A rowhouse fire in Southwest D.C. that displaced two adults and two children Sunday night has been pinned on a “lithium ion battery in an electrical mobility device,” in this case an electric dirt bike that was stored and charged inside.

The fire raised concerns from D.C. fire officials, who continue to warn that the increasing number of electric bikes and scooters — especially those bought online and shipped from China — could pose risks to residents, especially if they are charged indoors.

D.C. has experienced an increase in e-bike and scooter usage, and some significant fires: one in early 2024 displaced 23 people from their building in Northwest, and another in Northeast in 2025 temporarily left four people without a home.

The D.C. Council may soon take action. Members are expected to vote on a bill this fall that would require local retailers to only sell electric bikes and scooters (and their related battery components) that are specifically certified to avoid the types of risks that have led to fires. Similar legislation was adopted in New York in 2024, and lawmakers in San Francisco have discussed following suit this year.

In the meantime, D.C. fire officials are again advising caution. “Please stay safe. Charge larger devices (such as eBikes) away from your exit path and outside your home,” D.C. Fire and Emergency Medical Services said on social media.





FROM THE DISTRICT

U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro blasted a federal judge’s Monday decision to release the woman charged with vandalizing D.C.’s World War II Memorial, The Washington Post reports. Pirro told the Post that the woman, Melissa Farris, is “certainly” a flight risk if she’s not held until her trial. Farris is not from the D.C. area.

After being forced from the Kennedy Center, the National Symphony Orchestra announced it will play at six venues around the District for its 2026-27 season, The Associated Press reports.

The White House can paint tests on a small portion of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, a judge ruled this week. It’s a win for the Trump administration, which had been sued over its plans to repaint the building white to “aesthetically align” it with the White House next door. Plaintiffs argue that going through with the painting would damage the building and circumvent federal preservation laws.

“This is about whether the president of the United States must follow the law that everyone else follows when they're proposing a project that could harm a national historic landmark,” Greg Werkheiser, an attorney representing the plaintiffs, told NOTUS.





FROM VIRGINIA

Democratic Virginia Reps. Don Beyer and Suhas Subramanyam will meet today on Capitol Hill with Carolina Molina, the woman confronted last week by an armed ICE agent, to discuss “next steps” following the incident. Subramanyam previously told NOTUS that he is calling for criminal charges against the officer involved.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND

National Book Festival (2048x1366, AR: 1.50)
For fans of “yes, and”: Washington Improv Theater’s Improvapolooza at Studio Theatre, Wednesday through Sunday.

For Rock Creek Park loyalists: JazzDC AllStars at Carter Barron Amphitheater, Thursday.

For bookworms: National Book Festival at Washington Convention Center, Saturday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

A football nomad, new Commander Rasul Douglas has become a pro at hitting the ground running. Playing for his ninth NFL team in a 10-year career, the veteran defensive back — expected to be a key piece in Washington’s secondary this season — told NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson that he has approached this summer’s training camp the same way he has embraced every stop on his journey.

“You just get there, learn as much as you can, and then it's work,” he said.

Training camp update: For the first time since training camp kicked off July 29, center Nick Allegretti practiced with the team Tuesday. The timing couldn’t be any better: During Allegretti’s absence, Washington lost Pro Bowl left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps.

Allegretti said he stayed prepared by taking mental reps during his time on the sideline. “It's a cliche, but you really can get good work if you're locked in from the sideline or watching tape,” he said. “So, just trying to do that as much as I can to keep myself locked in. Because you can relax real easy and then come back out here and just a simple pressure can beat you.”

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Rangers, 8:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)

MLS: D.C. United vs. Revolution, 7:30 p.m. (Apple TV)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Tempo, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo courtesy of Library of Congress.

entries.title: Florida Person
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What we learned in Florida. The Senate runoff in South Carolina is getting spiky. Democrats asking for Republican help. We spoke to the lawmaker who got the most bills passed this Congress. A lot of people have quit on Scott Bessent. And: Rep. Richard Neal vs. the age question. 





THE LATEST

#Resistance is over, but there’s a new resistance. The Democrats weren’t likely to win the Senate race in Florida this year, but it’s clear now many of their voters want to cast a different kind of protest vote than expected. Alex Vindman, the former national security staffer whose testimony led to Donald Trump’s first impeachment, lost the Democratic primary to DSA-backed state lawmaker Angie Nixon, despite raising $16.3 million to her less than $1 million.

The shock result led to a lot of online mocking of the #Resistance figures who have struggled this year, like George Conway, who was among the many losers of the Democratic primary to replace Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-New York). “SleazeBag Vindman loses tonight to a Radical Left Lunatic. How cool is that???” Trump posted.

A certain subset of Democratic strategists were excited about guys like Vindman because they could easily be billed as the kind of fightin’ Democrat they presume the base wants. That theory appears to have actually been correct in Florida, but it was the fight itself the strategists were wrong about. Nixon is another full-throated critic of Israel, another candidate promising structural change, another one unafraid to say her own party’s leaders have fallen short.

This is the kind of resistance a lot of Democratic voters are interested in — and they want everyone to know it.

But not all of them. It was a good night for other mainline Democrats in Florida. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz absolutely crushed the field in her closely watched primary, while centrist Rep. Jared Moskowitz made easy work of his own DSA-backed challenger.

Republicans basically got the results the party wanted. Rep. Byron Donalds won the gubernatorial primary handily, and the incendiary James Fishback came in a distant third. Embattled Rep. Cory Mills lost his primary. But another candidate Trump endorsed went down, this time in the 19th Congressional District. Local media owner Jim Schwartzel won that primary.

Oh, one other thing: There were very few polls of the Democratic Senate primary, so this time the prediction markets got called out for being Wrong. And wrong they really were.

Open tabs: DOJ Plans to Deploy a ‘Historic Number’ of Midterm Election Monitors (NOTUS); US Navy destroyer with 300 sailors aboard broke down for four days in the Pacific (AP); Arrest warrant issued then dropped for Jill Stein (NY Post); FBI: 2025 had biggest violent-crime drop in 90 years (Axios)





From South Carolina


Going negative: Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina has not been in the job long, but she quipped like a pro last night during the Republican Senate runoff debate. “I think you’re confused because I don’t know if you want to be in South Carolina or Washington, because you said you wanted to go to Washington to clean up the swamp, then you wanted to come back to South Carolina to run for governor,” she said to her opponent, Rep. Ralph Norman. “Now you want to go back to Washington again to clean up the swamp.”

And that was the nice Graham. The debate crowd actually gasped when she said to Norman, “Apparently you hired illegal immigrants,” as part of a back-and-forth about education. Norman appeared rattled, and dismissed it as “a Democrat talking line.”

Also dismissing Graham: many pro-lifers. A rift in the anti-abortion movement is playing out over who its best advocate is in the runoff, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports.

From the campaign trail


First on NOTUS: A Democrat runs against everybody in Montana. “While politicians in both parties get rich on our backs, our problems only get worse,” Democrat Sam Forstag says in a new TV ad hitting the airwaves in Montana’s 1st Congressional District today, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton tells us. Forstag is running to replace Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, and is a big part of Democrats’ hopes of rebuilding a base in rural states.

Trend alert: Democrats with Republican friends. Democratic candidates in red and purple places are turning to Republican validators to help them win statewide contests, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic reports. “Endorsements overall are overrated,” Jeff Flake, the former Republican senator from Arizona who just endorsed Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Georgia), told Igor. “But cross-party endorsements can help and have helped in the past.”

From the Hill


Rep. Nick Begich’s big Congress: The Alaska Republican freshman has gotten six bills to the president’s desk so far this Congress, which is more than anyone else in the current session. NOTUS’ Mark Alfred spoke to the 119th’s most successful lawmaker — and Begich had his talking points ready to go: “We’ve received a lot of cooperation and recognition on both sides of the aisle that Alaska-specific issues really belong in the hands of the Alaskan that was sent to Congress to represent Alaska,” he said.





THE BIG ONE

Primary Complaints. “Let’s put this way: I think there’s a tendency for challengers in congressional elections to want the public to come to believe that history started on the day they were born,” Rep. Richard Neal, a Democrat who has represented Massachusetts in Congress since 1989, told NOTUS’ Kate Nocera recently.

It’s a portrait of a party elder who has had just about enough with the Democratic fight about age. Neal has his own young, progressive challenger: high school teacher Jeromie Whalen. Whalen is 39, Neal is 77. Whalen says Neal has become the embodiment of Washington and is MIA in the district.

Neal is unbothered, pointing to the millions of dollars he’s directed to Western Massachusetts. “I mean, it’s what every challenger says,” he told Kate. “There’s not a lot of evidence to support it.”

This posture has worked for Neal when it hasn’t for other longtime Democrats. Will it work this cycle? Whalen’s doing the thing — large social media profile, field-heavy campaigning, generally showing off his youthful energy — but he’s on his own. The national groups that have backed progressive upstarts are leaving Neal alone. Whalen, too, is unbothered. “Look, AOC beat Joe Crowley and only raised $300,000, and that was in New York City,” he said.

Which style of hubris will win out? We’ll have to wait until the Sept. 1 primary. There’s zero public polling of the race so far. Whalen says he can pull it off. Neal has never even uttered Whalen’s name publicly once. When Kate asked him about that, he called her “perceptive.”

Add to it that Bessent has gone through at least three separate chiefs of staff so far, and it’s time to start wondering what’s going on.

entries.title: This Freshman Congressman Is Out-Legislating All Other Lawmakers
entries.summary: Nick Begich has shepherded more stand-alone bills to Trump’s desk than any other lawmaker this session.
entries.content:
The 119th Congress is on track to be one of the least productive in recent history, furthering the trend of fewer and fewer bills ever becoming law. Setting aside the renaming of buildings such as post offices, most House lawmakers have never introduced a bill that a president signed into law.

Rep. Nick Begich III, the freshman lawmaker representing Alaska, is bucking that trend.

Since he entered the House in January 2025, six of Begich’s bills have passed through Congress and earned President Donald Trump’s signature — outpacing every one of his congressional colleagues.

Begich in part attributes his legislative win streak to geography.

“We’ve received a lot of cooperation and recognition on both sides of the aisle that Alaska-specific issues really belong in the hands of the Alaskan that was sent to Congress to represent Alaska,” Begich told NOTUS in an interview.

The Begich name is synonymous with Alaskan politics: The congressman’s grandfather Nick Begich Sr. also served as the state’s at-large representative. His uncle Mark was a U.S. senator from Alaska, and his other uncle Tom is currently running for the state’s governorship. (Unlike the congressman, the other Begiches are Democrats.)

In 2024, Nick Begich III defeated then-Rep. Mary Peltola, the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in half a century. Begich placed first in Tuesday’s open primary, coming in about 15 points ahead of his next closest rival, independent Bill Hill.

“In his first term, Nick Begich has proven to be an historically effective member of Congress,” Speaker Mike Johnson, who recently campaigned with Begich in Alaska, said in a statement to NOTUS. “Nick is a workhorse who has set an excellent example of how House Republicans are working to deliver for American families.”

Most of the bills Begich introduced that became law focus on specific issues affecting various Alaskan populations. They passed via voice vote or a near-unanimous roll-call vote before Trump signed them.

One excludes settlement trust payments made to Alaska Natives from counting against their eligibility for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program payments.

Another extends the window in which Alaska Native Vietnam veterans are able to claim federal land by five years, into 2030.

Yet another allows Cape Fox Corporation to claim its land settlement at a more suitable location within the Tongass National Forest.

“That's a bill that had been brought up 11 times over 22 years, and we were able to move that bill out of the House for the first time,” Begich said of the long-stalled Cape Fox legislation. “Our objective was to use this political window that we have, this trifecta in government, to move this priority through, and we were able to finally do that through a lot of work by my team and a lot of work by myself and others.”

With the slim GOP majority, his perch on the House Natural Resources Committee and the backing of a president more than eager to “drill, baby, drill,” Begich has unwound Biden-era roadblocks to oil and gas production using a legislative tactic that will be immensely difficult for Democrats to counter even if they win back both chambers after November.

The Republican trifecta “really opened the aperture for Alaska, not just to develop these resources through the actions of an executive administration, but to lock in durably our ability to develop those resources on an ongoing basis, regardless of where the president is,” Begich said.
https://x.com/RepNickBegich/status/1999296590411104304?s=20 Late in his presidency, Joe Biden took a number of actions to disallow new oil and gas drilling in Alaska. One such rule shielded 21 regions of the 3.6 million acre Central Yukon region in Alaska’s interior from development. Another effectively barred new oil and gas leases in the 1.6 million acre Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain, limiting activity in the refuge to 400,000 acres, the statutory minimum, most of which were subject to additional restrictions.

Begich introduced two Congressional Review Act resolutions undoing those protections. Neither was subject to the Senate filibuster, allowing Republicans to pass them with simple majorities in both chambers. The federal government is now disallowed from reinstating new restrictions that are substantially the same unless Congress passes them into law, a process that would be subject to the filibuster.

“We’ve been able to durably repeal a number of the regulatory structures that were imposed upon Alaska during the Biden administration,” Begich said.

Democrats warned of the environmental impacts of new drilling leases, and forced a recorded vote tally on both measures.

“This misguided bill would lock in oil and gas development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, an area known to the Gwich’in people as the sacred place where life begins,” Rep. Jared Huffman (D-California), the ranking member on the Natural Resources Committee, said at the time of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge measure. “The 9,000-strong Gwich’in Nation, whose subsistence and culture depend on the caribou herd ... making any disruption not only a threat to biodiversity but also an assault on indigenous livelihoods and traditions.”

Begich said Democrats’ opposition stemmed from a deference to activists and donors.

“I don't go to Connecticut to try to shut their forestry down, but those same members vote against Alaska's ability to develop those same industries in our state, and it's a little duplicitous,” Begich said. “You have to look at the donor base and the activist base within the Democrat Party to really understand perhaps where those motivations come from.”

The Alaska delegation’s fingerprints are apparent on Republicans’ first reconciliation bill, which mandated new onshore and offshore oil and gas leasing and new coal mining leases. The state is set to reap “70% of federal royalties” from many of the new leases.

“Congressman Begich has been an incredibly effective partner in delivering results for Alaskans,” Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan told NOTUS. “What we do as a delegation matters — we need Alaska’s representatives in both chambers rowing in the same direction, and Nick works overtime to get practical Alaska priorities across the goal line in the House.”

One area where Begich isn’t meeting resistance to his energy policies is from once-and-future political rivals like Peltola, who has mounted a formidable challenge to Sullivan. Online, her campaign proudly touts her support for oil and gas projects over the objections of other Democrats: “Mary has always been a champion for Alaska energy, consistently standing up to anyone — including Joe Biden — to promote oil and gas development.”

Begich’s independent opponent Hill vows to “go to bat for getting the most out of our oil and natural gas.” Hill is endorsed by Democrat Matt Schultz, who suspended his campaign in July. The independent won't explicitly say which party he’d caucus with.

“Congressman Nick Begich hit the ground running in Congress and is already delivering commonsense wins for Alaska and the American people,” NRCC spokesperson Zach Bannon told NOTUS. “From unleashing energy and expanding access to housing to standing up for Alaska Natives, Begich has proven he’ll always put Alaska first. He’s delivering results, and he’s just getting started.”

(The DCCC and Alaska Democrats did not respond to requests for comment for this article.)

Before he was first elected, Begich decried the abrasive politics that have defined much of the Trump era.

“The political environment has gotten so caustic that we’re forgetting that we’re all in the same boat together,” he told KCAW in August 2024. “But what is different about yesterday versus today is that while we did disagree, we were able to go out afterward and have dinner together, have a drink together, and respect one another.”

Three days after taking public office, Begich dispensed with that sentiment.

“Joe Biden is a son of a bitch,” he said online after the outgoing president announced a ban on offshore drilling around Alaska and much of the United States’ coastline. The “Democrat machine is more than happy to sacrifice us all in the name of their sanctimonious, socialist-driven, climate science™ religion.”

Begich doesn’t buy into climate science writ large, although he acknowledges the state has gotten warmer.

“Things have been good; it's been probably in the 60s and low 70s, which is just at the peak of heat for us,” Begich said of the weather while on recess from Congress. “It was actually the first-ever heat advisory in Anchorage. It hit like 70-something degrees, and they decided it was too hot for people.”

The state is also “the world’s HOTTEST oil exploration target,” Begich wrote online, borrowing a turn of phrase from the president he’s closely aligned himself with.
TrumpMap (1536x1023, AR: 1.50)Begich’s votes have kept him in Trump’s good graces. Unlike his Senate counterparts, he steered clear of the outcry that followed the president’s renaming of Denali and, as a member of the lower chamber, has not had to involve himself in the bitter fight over the filibuster and SAVE America Act that has led Trump to rail against Sen. Lisa Murkowski.

“I’m against Murkowski … she’s not good," Trump said recently, a sharp contrast to his repeated praise of Begich, having called him a "warrior,” at multiple gatherings.

“Nick. Thank you, Nick. Good job. Good job. Good, good votes,” Trump said during a cryptocurrency event last year. “I just saw a great poll on you, huh? Very good. Congratulations, Nick.”

entries.title: Commanders’ Rasul Douglas Is Good at Getting Up to Speed
entries.summary: On his ninth NFL team, the veteran defensive back knows how to adapt and contribute.
entries.content:
Over the span of a month and a half back in 2021, Rasul Douglas earned a lot of airline miles.

The defensive back was released from the Raiders on Aug. 23, and signed with the Texans two days later. Less than a week after that, he was released again. Three days went by before Douglas was added to the Cardinals practice squad, a marriage that lasted an eternity (33 days) compared to his previous stops. He then joined Green Bay, where he’d stay for the next two seasons.

Douglas has signed with nine teams over his 10-year career, never staying in one place for longer than three years. He signed with the Commanders on July 9, more than a month after offseason practices started and just a few weeks before training camp. With Washington already facing some injury issues at the position, Douglas may be called upon to step up as a late-arriving starter, something he has done many times in his career.

To the average person, that’s asking a lot. For Douglas, it’s just another day in the NFL.

“You just get there, learn as much as you can, and then it's work,” he said.

The Commanders signed Douglas last month after second-year cornerback Trey Amos, a presumed starter, missed all of June’s organized team activities and minicamp as he recovers from a broken fibula.

Compared to last year, this last-minute signing felt more like an early-bird special for Douglas. He signed with the Dolphins on Aug. 26, 2025, and played in the team’s first game on Sept. 7. In Week 2, he started. Despite having little time to learn the playbook, Douglas had one of his best seasons as a pro. His 13 pass breakups were one short of tying a career high.

“Last year I came to Miami two days before the first game,” Douglas said. “[By] the 10th play of that game, I'm out there playing, and it was like, ‘I don't know what's going on.’ Coach said, ‘Look, I'm just gonna tell you [what to do] before every play.’ So, it's different. You just gotta be ready.”

That stop in Miami (the team did not renew his one-year deal) was just the latest of many short stays over the years.

The West Virginia product spent three years with the Eagles after being selected in the third round of the 2017 draft. He then signed with the Panthers for the 2020 season, playing in his first game two weeks after agreeing to a one-year deal. On April 19, 2021, he signed with the Raiders but was released four months later after getting into what he calls an “altercation” with a teammate.

Rasul Douglas Bills AP - 24294761245506 (2790x1860, AR: 1.50)
He was on the Texans roster for a week before testing positive for COVID-19 and getting cut. That started the chain of events that led him to Green Bay. He signed with the Packers on Oct. 6, 2021, and played 11 days later. After two seasons, he was traded to the Bills on Oct. 31, 2023, and played for them the very next week.

He said teammates and coaches have been invaluable in getting him up to speed once he joins a roster. This summer, Douglas can often be seen getting extra reps after training camp, working with receivers and defensive backs on guarding releases and eye discipline.

Douglas admits that, early in his career, he didn’t have the best study habits. Watching film in Philadelphia, he’d get distracted by the receivers’ highlight plays and neglect to pay attention to what the defensive back did wrong.

But during the 2020 and 2021 seasons he worked with defensive back coaches Jason Simmons (Panthers) and Jerry Gray (Packers), who taught Douglas — in ways he understood — how to properly study film and learn defensive schemes. Gray, currently the defensive pass-game coordinator for the 49ers, encouraged Douglas to lean into his aggressive playmaking style.

“Everybody knows I have good rock feels,” Douglas said, referring to his ability to spot a receiver’s route intentions. “So you might get a double move every once in a while, but that's just to keep you honest and make sure you’re actually looking at the guy instead of looking at the concepts.”

Commanders coach Dan Quinn said he didn’t realize Douglas had so much experience as a last-minute starter when the team signed him. But Quinn is confident Douglas can lean on his skills while he learns new terminology.

“Because of his length, he can maybe get to some spaces that others don't,” Quinn said. “I think he's got good patience on the ball that goes down the field.”

Rasul Douglas camp AP - 26210558870673 (2450x1633, AR: 1.50)
Those skills only seem to get sharper with time. From 2018 to 2020, Douglas allowed a 63.4% completion percentage and 107.1 passer rating as the closest defender, according to Pro Football Reference. Last season in Miami, Douglas allowed a 54.5% completion percentage and 73.0 passer rating.

“It's always good to have a guy like that in your room and just listen to him when he talks and just be on the same page and catch him up as quickly as possible because we know he can contribute,” safety Quan Martin said.

Amos returned to practice on Aug. 7 but lasted just two practices before injuring his ankle. Douglas, who has gotten most of the first-team reps at corner in Amos’ absence, may well have to step in as a starter for Washington come Week 1.

All this movement isn’t something Douglas will ever really get used to. But at this point in his career, he understands that playing the game he loves might mean keeping the Zillow app on his homescreen.

“It's been hard, but I mean, it's what it takes to play football,” he said. “So, if you want to do it and you love doing it, you’re going to do it. Luckily, I'm not moving a lot of people. It's really just me. So, it's all right.”

entries.title: Voters Are Ousting Longtime Incumbents. So Why Is No One Talking About Richard Neal?
entries.summary: Neal has been in office for nearly four decades — but in an under-the-radar primary, voters have to decide if the power he’s accumulated is enough to reelect him.
entries.content:
SPRINGFIELD, Mass. — Seven House Democrats have lost their seats to primary challengers this year. Rep. Richard Neal, the 77-year-old Massachusetts Democrat who was first elected in 1988, is not worried he will join them.

Neal has spent decades accumulating power, and, as the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, he has been able to run the party’s policy apparatus in the House. His campaign says he’s donated or fundraised $5.5 million for competitive races to help Democrats win back the majority in November. And he remains confident that his longstanding ties to voters and his seniority — which is ultimately power in Congress — will make his September primary here against Jeromie Whalen, a 39-year-old public school teacher, an easy one for him to win.

But as several of his Democratic colleagues recently discovered, seniority is not the political shield it once was, as voters this year have shown their willingness to toss out decades of accumulated experience. They have opted instead for generational change.

If he does lose? Establishment Democrats would have a hard time writing it off as just another cranky electorate showing an aging lawmaker the door. Neal’s stamp on major Democratic legislation from his perch on Ways and Means has benefited Western Massachusetts to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. If voters decide that isn’t worth preserving, the problem for the party gets bigger than age. It would suggest that the traditional bargain with voters — keep sending me back and I’ll accumulate power and money on your behalf — may be breaking down.

Neal isn’t even entertaining the possibility.

“Let's put this way: I think there's a tendency for challengers in congressional elections to want the public to come to believe that history started on the day they were born,” he told me in a recent interview. Previous challengers have “really been unable to fracture, nevermind break” his longstanding relationships in the district.

* * *

Massachusetts’ 1st Congressional District is easy to characterize as a deep-blue seat of liberal college enclaves ripe for progressive insurgency. On the ground it’s more complicated. The district includes Springfield and its working-class, post-industrial neighborhoods, struggling former mill towns and rural farming communities. There is considerable wealth here, but also deep poverty and communities hollowed out by the opioid epidemic.

Neal’s ability to secure funding for the district has been key to his success even when the headwinds have been bad for incumbents.

“Richie has always maintained a close relationship with the district,” said a source close to the Neal campaign. “You won’t catch him sleeping … but more than that, Richie’s a liberal. Like I think some people on the left want to run a campaign against a Blue Dog but Richie is a pro-labor, pro-worker, pro-Social Security Democrat, and he’s been rock solid on that.”

Neal has only had a handful of primary challengers and even fewer competitive ones. His last real challenge was in 2020 against the young, progressive mayor of Holyoke, Alex Morse, who was backed by Justice Democrats. Justice Democrats spent mightily against Neal, and he still won by double digits.

Confidence from those past wins has carried into this cycle. The lawmaker says comparisons between losing incumbents are the result of the “national media” looking for a narrative where there isn’t one. But some of the similarities between losing incumbents are difficult to ignore.

Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colorado), a nearly 30-year veteran of the House, lost her June primary to 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros. DeGette had handily won her primary in 2022 and didn’t even field a challenger in 2024. Rep. John Larson (D-Connecticut) was ousted last week after 14 terms in the House by Luke Bronin, the 47-year-old former mayor of Hartford. Before this year, Larson hadn’t faced a Democratic primary challenger since his first race for Congress, 28 years ago.
AP 23143678030664 (8471x5647, AR: 1.50)DeGette and Larson essentially made the same bet Neal is making now: that voters would value their seniority more than they wanted someone new. Both, like Neal, spent decades building organizations and relationships in their districts. Both argued that their seniority would position them for powerful committee posts if Democrats win the House in November.

Neal isn’t promising voters that his seniority could translate into power. He has already had it and wielded it plenty on their behalf.

“I've authored major legislation that has benefited people. I brought back billions of dollars to the state of Massachusetts — not millions, not tens of millions, billions of dollars,” he said. “I mean, I wrote the American Rescue Act with [Nancy] Pelosi, if you look at the Butch Lewis Act on the pension front … I mean, these are the things that clearly are breaking through.”

“It's interesting to me that the Inflation Reduction Act is the most consequential environmental legislation in American history and it came out of the Ways and Means Committee when I was chairman — $412 billion worth of tax credits, and it’s working,” he added.

* * *

The Democratic Party’s existential crisis over age is especially prevalent this election cycle. Of the Democratic incumbents who have lost, five were over the retirement age.

Enter Whalen, who spends his days driving around in a bright yellow Toyota Cargo Van from 1988 — the same year Neal was first elected to Congress — that looks like it’s held together with Scotch tape, and bears the license plate “VANANA.” His lawn signs match the van’s yellow paint; a billboard over Interstate 91 instructs voters to “trust the man with the yellow van.”

Whalen often likes to say that he’s been alive almost as long as Neal has been in office. His staff skews young too: His communications director, Joey Pisani, is entering his junior year of college and only just turned 20 years old. Whalen is attempting to visit and knock on doors in all 83 municipalities before the election, which means a lot of time in the van.
JeromieWhalen_IPL-0002 copy.jpg (4000x2666, AR: 1.50)JeromieWhalen_IPL-0001 copy.jpg (3924x2616, AR: 1.50)“The other day when I was driving, Metallica’s ‘Ride the Lightning’ came on,” he said. “I go, ‘Has Richie ever heard this song? Does Richie know who Metallica is?’ It's just something small but like, is Richie plugged into society? Not just pop culture, but is he plugged into society and concerns and issues in any way that would be something where he would understand what’s happening out here?”

On paper, Whalen reads as engineered in a lab to attract the national groups that have spent years trying to dislodge entrenched Democrats. He supports “Medicare for All,” wants to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement and refuses corporate PAC money (his primary critique of Neal is that his fundraising is driven almost entirely by PAC money). Justice Democrats, which did not respond to a request for comment, once called Neal “the epitome of a corporate Democrat.”

But the national cavalry isn’t running to Whalen. Neal’s victory in 2020 was so decisive, no one has really bothered to try and take him out since.

Now Whalen thinks the district is open to an alternative. While his name ID is likely extremely low, his consistent social media presence has racked up hundreds of thousands of views in the last three months. His campaign is extremely proud of its ground game, citing more than 50,000 voters reached according to internal data. Lawn signs don’t vote, but Whalen signs have been out everywhere since April, where Neal’s only just started cropping up in August. Through Whalen’s travels around the district, he says the Neal true believers just aren’t out here.

“When knocking doors, the most resounding message I’ve heard is, ‘It’s time.’ Richard Neal’s base has always been an older generation of voters, and that base has dwindled as people have passed away, retired to Florida or moved elsewhere,” Whalen said.

Those who are still here, he says, “believe it’s time to pass the torch.”

Voters at his events say as much.

“I’m just not happy with the status quo,” said Claire Murphy, 72, a former Neal voter at a Whalen event. “It’s just time for some new blood.”

Her husband, Bob, interjected.

“Look, we can say ‘Thank you for serving the community, thank you for serving the government, but it’s time for him to hang it up,” he said. “It’s time for new ideas and younger blood.”

Whalen campaigns almost exclusively in T-shirts, shorts and hiking boots but is not above a costume. For a Fourth of July parade in East Longmeadow, he donned a full Uncle Sam getup to run down the route.
JeromieWhalen_IPL-0022.jpg (4000x3000, AR: 1.33)Whalen had been thinking about a run since Donald Trump was reelected in 2024. He saved up some money and took a leave of absence from his public school job so he could make campaigning his fulltime gig — his wife works in finance in New York to support them, traveling back and forth most weeks, something he readily acknowledges is something most people can’t do. In February 2025, tragedy struck Whalen’s family when his older brother Chris died by suicide. Six months later, Whalen announced his campaign.

“I made a commitment in the classroom a long time ago to make the world a better place, and now I am making a commitment to my brother’s legacy to do the same,” he said.

He approaches campaigning with the energy of a golden retriever puppy, but things shift when he talks about Chris and the toll severe mental illness can take.

“At the center of everything is joy,” he resolves, wiping tears away. “I think that's the biggest influence that you can have on the world is just making it a better place, aside from legislation, aside from any governmental procedures or protocol.”

A thousand people showed up for the wake, Whalen says, something he’s reminded of almost daily when people bring up his brother as he knocks on doors in the district.

Joy and legacy might be the touchstones for his campaign approach, but the dynamics of the race hinge around something more concrete: money.

Neal is heading into the final weeks of the primary with roughly $4 million and has already spent around $350,000 on mailers, television and digital advertising — about $100,000 more than Whalen has raised during the entire campaign.
IMG_0441 copy.jpg (5712x3808, AR: 1.50)Whalen argues that money isn’t destiny, especially in a cheap media market with no public polling.

“Look, AOC beat Joe Crowley and only raised $300,000 and that was in New York City,” Whalen stressed in an interview during a day of canvassing.

Talking about money also gives Whalen the opportunity to make his favorite Neal criticism. Only a fraction of Neal’s fundraising this year comes from small-dollar donors, and more than half of his money this cycle comes from PACs, according to Federal Election Commission data analyzed by OpenSecrets.

“The money I’ve raised is overwhelmingly going to other Democratic candidates and the DCCC, but I’m not going to disarm,” Neal said in defense. “I had hundreds of thousands of dollars in outside money spent against me in the race against Morse.”

Neal also brushes off Whalen’s other big criticism: that he is not available in the district.

“I mean, it's what every challenger says,” he said. “It's the rhetoric that's embraced, and generally, there's not a lot of evidence to support it.”

* * *

There’s no public polling on the race, so the question of who has momentum is really a game of vibes. Nonpartisan district polling is practically nonexistent. In light of Larson’s loss, some more attention has come Neal’s way, especially as another generational fight plays out in the Senate primary between incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, 80, and Rep. Seth Moulton, 47.

A new poll from UMass Amherst showed Markey up significantly over Moulton, and voters seemed to not care about his age, with 91% of primary voters viewing his experience as an asset rather than a liability. But those aren’t tea leaves Neal should read into all that much either, the poll’s director, Tatishe Nteta, said.

“The Moulton-Markey race is a little different because the challenger is moderate and is sort of viewed in the most positive way as, um, ambitious,” he said. “I don’t think those are the dynamics with Neal and Whalen. Senate primary voters in Massachusetts value progressivism over all else.”

The Neal and Whalen race is ultimately a test of if people are going to be willing to give up the kind of “power, influence and bacon” Neal has been able to wield, Nteta added.

The final stretch of the campaign will include a 30-minute debate on Aug. 26, after early voting has begun. Neal, meanwhile, is flexing his ability to show just how entrenched his support actually is.
IMG_0439 copy.jpg (8588x5355, AR: 1.60)George Bruce, an 82-year-old Springfield resident, said he was asked to attend a recent African Community Festival, where Neal appeared and was flanked by dozens of Black community leaders, in 100-degree heat to show support for Neal because he’s known Neal his “entire life.”

“He never forgot where he came from, so no matter what color or creed you were, he was always there for us,” Bruce said. “Richie is a strong man, and I appreciate him.”

Timothy Paul, a pastor and founder of a Springfield church, was the first to greet Neal at the festival.

“We’re just here to help him because we remember what he’s done for our community,” Paul said. “And we’re going to help other people remember.”

Neal has the money and the infrastructure and is projecting so much confidence, he’s never uttered Whalen’s name publicly, calling this reporter “perceptive” when it was pointed out to him.

“I think that if one dresses up as a leprechaun, or dresses up as, uh, let's see, Uncle Sam, you’re trying to create a sensation on social media and that is something that's generally not gonna get you elected to Congress,” he said.

entries.title: Nearly Half of Trump’s Treasury Appointees Have Left
entries.summary: While many agencies have had turnover, the Treasury Department has seen an exodus of Senate-confirmed officials.
entries.content:
The Treasury Department has seen a dramatic exodus of President Donald Trump's own appointees, outpacing the turnover of any other recent administration.

Since the start of the second Trump administration, seven of 16 Treasury appointees confirmed by the Senate — or roughly 44% — have either quit or been pushed out of their positions, according to the Partnership for Public Service, a nonpartisan watchdog. That does not account for the turnover in Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s office; he has had at least three different chiefs of staff since the beginning of the administration.

At least four of the seven top Treasury officials left after disagreements with the White House over demands to stretch, if not violate, tax law. Those disputes included Treasury resistance to a controversial push to use taxpayer data as part of the administration’s immigration crackdown, as well as the president’s push to establish a $1.8 billion fund to compensate allies as part of a deal with the IRS to drop any past or future tax audits of the president and his family. (The “anti-weaponization” fund was later dropped due to resistance from Senate Republicans.)

“They’re asking them to do stuff that is well beyond the norm, and for some things that may or may not be legal,” said Mark Mazur, who held senior positions at the IRS under both parties and was acting assistant secretary for tax policy in Biden's Treasury Department. “A lot of these people expect to have a career after this administration, and being disbarred would be a bad thing for them.”

A spokeswoman for the Treasury Department declined to comment.

Bessent is widely regarded as more competent than most of Trump’s Cabinet, and has bridged the divisions on the right better than many of the president’s aides. His allies on the right credit him with doing more to execute Trump’s agenda than Steven Mnuchin, the president’s first treasury secretary, and also argue his hard-charging Wall Street style is an asset.

An enormous number of responsibilities currently fall under Bessent’s remit, from managing the risks of artificial intelligence to crafting economic sanctions on Iran as part of the U.S. war effort.

“Secretary Bessent is doing a fantastic job delivering the President’s agenda for the American people,” said Nick Solheim, the chief operations officer at American Moment, a pro-Trump advocacy and recruitment organization. “He and many of the appointees at Treasury have made a great sacrifice leaving the private sector to take roles in public service so that we have a financial system that works for every American.”

Still, the level of churn among his senior ranks — far higher than that under any other treasury secretary this century — shows that even Republican tax officials have balked at Trump’s demands on the IRS, which is a part of the Treasury.

The departures also raise questions about whether gaps in the Treasury’s ranks could undermine its response to an economic crisis or other emergency.

By this point in their terms, the Obama and Biden administrations had lost zero Senate-confirmed appointees, according to the Partnership for Public Service. The Bush administration and the first Trump administration had lost two each by this point.

Like many agencies under the second Trump administration, the Treasury and IRS have also lost thousands of career employees up and down its ranks. The number of IRS employees has fallen by about a quarter, and Treasury has lost senior officials including David A. Lebryk, who had served in senior Treasury positions under six administrations, and Andrea Gacki, who served as director of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

But many agencies under Trump have pushed out many of their career officials with far less turnover among the senior political ranks. For instance, the State Department has lost only one Senate-confirmed appointee, the Partnership for Public Service found. The Defense Department has only lost two senior Senate-confirmed officials.

Among those to depart Treasury’s senior ranks were Republicans in good standing with the party. While the exact reasons for their exits are unclear, they came after disagreeing with directives from the White House.

John Hurley, a Trump donor who was appointed undersecretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, left the department after expressing concerns about a White House-led crackdown to target international payments from Minneapolis, though there were other factors at play in his departure. Several legal experts said the Minneapolis order to scrutinize immigrant payments violated constitutional protections against unreasonable search and seizure.

Ken Kies, an assistant treasury secretary and acting IRS chief counsel, was forced out after objecting to a White House request that risked violating an IRS code limiting political interference in audits or taxpayer investigations, according to one person familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private conversation. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the circumstances behind his departure.

Billy Long, the Senate-confirmed IRS commissioner, was pushed out after objecting to demands that the IRS give confidential taxpayer information to the Department of Homeland Security.

The IRS had seven different acting commissioners last year: Danny Werfel, Douglas O’Donnell, Melanie Krause, Gary Shapley, Michael Faulkender, Long, and Bessent. Trump has not nominated a new commissioner. Frank J. Bisignano, who is also the commissioner of the Social Security Administration, is currently serving as the "chief executive officer" of the IRS, a new position with no apparent designation in law.

Brian Morrissey, the treasury general counsel, resigned hours after the Trump administration announced its plans for the $1.8 billion fund to make payments to Trump's political allies.

"People are really concerned about a job that they would normally see as the highlight of their career," said Nina Olson, the former head of the Taxpayer Advocate, a nonpartisan watchdog group. “What they are being asked to do appears to put them at risk of civil or criminal penalties.”

Tax experts and various former government officials have raised questions about the impact of the turnover. Daniel Bunn, president and CEO of the Tax Foundation, a conservative-leaning think tank, expressed concern that the absences could slow the process of writing the regulations necessary to implement the tax law Republicans approved last year.

“It’s a real risk to the policy legacy of the administration on tax to not have these roles filled with people that can make sure the policies get implemented in line with the legislation,” Bunn said. “Anytime you have gaps in the leadership structure it’s tough.”

Bessent has been more hands-off in drafting regulations than his predecessor Mnuchin, according to two former Treasury officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private interactions. With several posts all still open, much of that burden has fallen on a shrinking core of remaining officials.

"I'm an admirer of both Secretary Bessent and IRS Chief [Frank] Bisignano,” said Mark Everson, who ran the IRS during the Bush administration and also served under President Ronald Reagan. “That said, if leadership is stretched too thin it can be harder to keep the trains running on time and difficult to respond effectively in the event a crisis comes along and you need all hands on deck."
